Photograph: gillou70/Getty Images/iStockphoto France Call to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’ Protests and petitions planned amid growing concerns over impact of climate crisis on numbers of Alpine rodent Kim Willsher in Paris Wed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Animal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots. Open season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September, a few weeks before they go into a long winter hibernation. Although the marmot is not a threatened species in France , its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun. Pauline di Nicolantonio, the president of the Association for Justice for Savoie Animals (AJAS ), which has launched protests against marmot hunting for the last two years, said: “The question is a moral one. “When you tell people that hunting marmots is allowed in France, they are shocked. The marmot is extremely popular and symbolic in the Savoie where we are based and elsewhere in the Alps. You only have to go into any tourist office to see it’s the main logo or emblem.” Plant-eating marmots are spread across mountainous areas of Europe and North America. Most live in family groups organised by one dominant couple; when threatened they emit a high-pitched signal. In late summer and into autumn their bodies swell to up to 8kg as they stock up on food for a five- to six-month hibernation. There are 15 marmot species in the world and as wild game they were traditionally hunted for their meat, fat and fur. Today, hunting is allowed in certain states in the US and Canada, and in France, Switzerland and Austria but banned in Italy and Germany. An average of 1,000 marmots are shot in France each year. For generations of French children the marmot has been celebrated as the subject of folk tales and poems – one by Goethe set to music by Beethoven – the mascot of Alpine ski resorts and the sympathetic star of a popular television advert for a well-known brand of milk chocolate . In fact, the rodents’ cuddly reputation belies a bloodier reality; much of its waking life is spent in a vicious battle for dominance and territory that often involves killing its parents or children. View image in fullscreen Experts say they are seeing the breaking up of social groups of marmots. Photograph: Jean Christophe Verhaegen/AFP/Getty Images Christophe Bonenfant, a scientist at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CRNS) at the University of Lyon, studies marmots in the Grande Sassière alpine nature reserve . Evidence of the climate crisis in Europe is most evident in the Alps where rock faces are fissuring and glaciers shrinking at an unprecedented rate. Bonenfant and his colleague Rébecca Garcia have noticed the marmots’ domestic and territorial battles becoming increasingly brutal as the climate emergency destroys the animal’s “social stability”. They have also noted that while the animals are not listed as endangered, females are producing fewer marmot pups and a combination of the cycle of violence and smaller litters is leading to a steady drop in populations. “What we are seeing is the breaking up of social groups, which are lasting less long, and more rapid changes of dominant animals in those groups,” Bonenfant said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “As a herbivore the marmot is quite low down the food chain but its importance is as food for carnivores like eagles and foxes and from time to time badgers. It also makes galleried tunnels that contribute to the aeration of the soil. It’s not classified as a nuisance species.” He said of hunting: “It’s not a species that raises questions about conservation, so the root of the question is the morality of hunting animals, not just in France but everywhere, and why people enjoy killing animals for fun.” There are strict hunting regulations set by individual local authorities limiting the number of marmots that can be killed and the season dates, but AJAS wants a national ban similar to that introduced in Italy in 1992. French farmers claim the animals are a nuisance making holes in their fields causing damage to machinery. The National Hunters Federation says hunting marmots is “strictly supervised and regulated” and the open season lasts at most a month. “There is no justification for banning marmot hunting: the species is not threatened, there are no plans to classify it as a protected species and their numbers are on the rise.” Di Nicolantonio said: “We know they are affected by the climate crisis and the data is worrying. Hunters often commission scientific reports to say there are lots of marmots around to justify killing them. “Hunting them is cruel, absurd and unpopular but isn’t banned because it’s considered a tradition. In the past, we might have eaten marmots but now shooting them is simply recreational.” Explore more on these topics France Animals Hunting Wildlife Conservation Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

People search posters of those missing in Nepal flood Nepal-Tibet flood disaster ‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.11 EDT First published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google P osters of missing people line the wall of the hospital, the glue still fresh beneath. A schoolgirl smiling in her uniform; a beaming, chubby-cheeked baby; a couple smiling on their wedding day; a young man, hands on hips, atop a mountain peak; a young girl with flowing hair, peaking out from behind a door. These faces are just a fraction of the thousands who have not been seen since deadly flash floods coursed through the Himalayas and wiped away entire villages. By Saturday morning, the toll of the missing had risen to almost 3,000, in both Nepal and Tibet . View image in fullscreen Relatives search through lists of people reported missing outside the hospital in Kathmandu. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian So far, Nepal has recovered 669 bodies, but many remote areas have only been accessed by army helicopters on the hunt for survivors. Rescuers said it was too difficult to assess how many more people might be buried beneath the mud. The task of identifying the dead is also gargantuan. In the Nepalese city of Chitwan, the morgues have been overrun by the sheer number of bodies and a makeshift building has been set up to house the dead. Some of the bodies were carried so far down the river by the force of the floods, they were recovered in neighbouring India. 2:02 Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainer At Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, desperate relatives gathered in the hope of news. Four days on since the disaster struck, people continued to crowd round the police desk to register the names of missing family members. Hundreds of the injured are recovering in the hospital’s wards and people were frantically checking lists of patients, desperate to find a sign that their loved ones were still alive. View image in fullscreen Relatives look through the lists of missing flood victims at the teaching hospital. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian In the absence of information and with affected areas almost completely cut off, many families have resorted to making posters to appeal for information. Yavraj Lama said his sister, her husband and their two children were missing after their village of Jaydada, in Rusawa district, had been entirely washed away. His eyes filled with tears as he glued a photo of one-year-old Sijan Tawang, a baby in the arms of his mother, to the hospital wall. A picture of 12-year-old Sahil, his brother, hung next to it. “We are numb, we don’t have words to say how sad and distraught we are,” said Lama. “Our main focus is trying to find baby Sijan. He was so sweet and innocent; it’s impossible for us to think he is not with us any more. “But their whole village has disappeared,” he added, “so we have no hope left that any of them survived.” View image in fullscreen Monita Nepali, right, whose husband is missing, is comforted at the hospital in Kathmandu. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian Monita Nepali, 22, howled in grief as a poster of her missing husband Vishal Nepali, 30, was pinned to the hospital wall. They had married six months ago and his work as a driver regularly took him to the border between Nepal and Tibet. She had spoken to her husband an hour before the floods hit when he was out for a morning walk in Rusawa. He had promised to call her that evening, but his phone has been ever off since. “I don’t want to live on the face of this earth without him,” she said. Four days may have passed, Nepali said, but she had not stopped believing in her husband’s return. “I feel it in my heart he will come back.” 10:11 ‘Erased before their eyes’: desperate rescue efforts continue after Nepal-Tibet floods - The Latest For some families, the scale of the loss was too hard to comprehend. Tulmaya Tamang, 36, came to the hospital bearing posters of some of her 12 family members, including her five-month-old niece, who lived in a village in Rusawa and have not been seen since the floods. “Our family is under tremendous stress,” she said. “So many are gone, and those of us who are left behind are struggling.” As hopes for their survival faded, Tamang said they were now just hoping the bodies could be retrieved. “If we had the bodies, then at least we could have peace,” she said. “Otherwise, the family will never stop wondering and this pain will go on for a very long time.” At least 900 of those still missing were working on the vast hydropower projects along the Trishuli River corridor, high up in the Himalayas, which were decimated by the floods and mudslides. Many of the workers were low-paid labourers, including at least 63 from India. View image in fullscreen A Nepali soldier rescues a survivor from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA On Friday, dramatic footage showed Nepali soldiers pulling several survivors out through a thick wall of mud from a tunnel in the Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The Nepali army said they believed at least another 100 people were still trapped inside the tunnels, as well as dozens more trapped underground in the Trishuli-3 hydropower plant. Among those missing was 24-year-old Sujan Nepali, who had just finished his night shift at the hydropower project and was asleep in bed when the wall of water came gushing down the valley. At the hospital trauma centre in Nepal, his sister, Sushisha Maluwar, had returned anxiously every day to check if his name was listed. “We haven’t lost hope,” she said. “We are writing down his name at the hospitals and putting up his photographs everywhere, hoping that we might find him somewhere. Maybe he has already been rescued. Maybe he had managed to escape and survive.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal Tibet Flooding South and central Asia Natural disasters news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Number of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to nearly 3,000 as operations continue What we know about the Australians missing in the Nepal floods At least 90 Americans missing in Nepal flood among 2,000 unaccounted for ‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage Search continues as number missing in Nepal-Tibet floods rises to 2,478 – as it happened Families of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floods Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
